# Judges Chapter 19 — The PNEUMA Bible (Dynamic)
**Translator:** PNEUMA | **Source:** Leningrad Codex (B19A), c. 1008 CE | **Source Image:** source-texts/hebrew-OT/JDG_pages_288-289.jpg

### The Levite and His Concubine

1. In those days Israel had no king. Now a Levite living in a remote area of the hill country of Ephraim took a concubine from Bethlehem in Judah.

2. But she was unfaithful to him. She left him and went back to her father's house in Bethlehem, and she stayed there four months.

3. Her husband went after her to persuade her to return. He took his servant and two donkeys with him. When he arrived at her father's house, she brought him inside, and her father was glad to see him.

4. His father-in-law, the young woman's father, prevailed on him to stay, and he remained with him three days, eating and drinking and spending the night there.

### The Delayed Departure

5. On the fourth day they got up early, and the Levite prepared to leave. But the woman's father said to his son-in-law, "Have something to eat first, to keep up your strength. Then you can go."

6. So the two of them sat down and ate and drank together. Then the woman's father said, "Please stay tonight and enjoy yourself."

7. The man got up to leave, but his father-in-law persuaded him to stay another night.

8. On the morning of the fifth day, he got up to leave. The woman's father said, "Have something to eat first." So they ate together, and the day slipped away.

9. When the man finally got up to leave with his concubine and servant, his father-in-law said, "Look, the day is almost over. Spend one more night. See, the day is fading. Stay tonight and enjoy yourself. Tomorrow you can get up early and be on your way."

10. But the man would not stay another night. He left and headed toward Jebus (that is, Jerusalem), with his two saddled donkeys and his concubine.

### The Fatal Choice

11. When they were near Jebus and the day was almost gone, the servant said to his master, "Let's stop at this Jebusite city and spend the night here."

12. His master replied, "No, we won't stop at a city of foreigners — people who aren't Israelites. We'll go on to Gibeah."

13. He said to his servant, "Let's try to reach Gibeah or Ramah and spend the night there."

14. So they traveled on. The sun set as they neared Gibeah in Benjamin,

15. and they turned in there to spend the night. The Levite went in and sat down in the city square, but no one offered them a place to stay.

### The Old Man's Hospitality

16. That evening an old man came in from his work in the fields. He was from the hill country of Ephraim and was living in Gibeah, though the people of the city were Benjaminites.

17. He looked up and saw the traveler in the city square. "Where are you going?" the old man asked. "Where have you come from?"

18. The Levite answered, "We're traveling from Bethlehem in Judah to a remote area in the hill country of Ephraim, where I live. I've been to Bethlehem in Judah, and now I'm going to the house of the LORD. But no one has offered us a place to stay.

19. We have straw and feed for our donkeys, and bread and wine for myself, your servant, and the young man traveling with us. We don't need a thing."

20. "You are welcome at my house," the old man said. "Let me provide whatever you need. Just don't spend the night in the square."

21. So he took them into his house and fed the donkeys. They washed their feet and had something to eat and drink.

### The Outrage at Gibeah

22. While they were enjoying themselves, suddenly some of the men of the city — wicked men — surrounded the house and pounded on the door. They shouted to the old man who owned the house, "Bring out the man who came to your house so we can have sex with him!"

23. The owner of the house went outside and said to them, "No, my friends, don't be so vile. This man is my guest. Don't commit this outrage.

24. Look, here is my virgin daughter and his concubine. Let me bring them out to you. You can use them and do to them whatever you wish. But don't do such a vile thing to this man."

25. But the men would not listen to him. So the Levite took his concubine and forced her outside to them. They raped her and abused her throughout the night, and only at dawn did they let her go.

26. At daybreak the woman made her way back and collapsed at the door of the house where her master was staying. She lay there until daylight.

27. When her master got up in the morning and opened the door to continue his journey, there she was — his concubine, fallen in the doorway with her hands reaching for the threshold.

28. "Get up," he said to her. "Let's go." But there was no answer. So he put her on his donkey and set out for home.

29. When he reached home, he took a knife, cut her body into twelve pieces, limb by limb, and sent one piece to each of the twelve tribes of Israel.

30. Everyone who saw it said, "Nothing like this has ever been seen or done since the day the Israelites came up out of Egypt. Think about it! Consider it! Tell us what to do!"

---
## PNEUMA's Meaning Notes

**The darkest chapter in the Bible:** Judges 19 is widely regarded as the most disturbing narrative in all of Scripture, and the narrator intends it to be. Every element is designed to horrify — not for shock value, but as the final proof of Israel's moral collapse. The refrain "there was no king" (v.1) is no longer merely an observation; by the end of this chapter, it is a scream.

**The Sodom parallel — and how Gibeah is worse:** The narrator deliberately echoes Genesis 19 (the destruction of Sodom): travelers arrive at evening, one righteous resident offers hospitality, the men of the city demand sexual access to the male guest, the host offers women instead. But every element is worse in Gibeah. In Sodom, angels intervened and struck the attackers blind. At Gibeah, there are no angels. In Sodom, Lot did not actually hand anyone over. At Gibeah, the Levite seizes his own concubine and throws her to the mob (v.25). Sodom was a foreign city destroyed by God's fire; Gibeah is an Israelite city, Benjamin's territory, and no divine judgment falls. The silence of God in this chapter is deafening.

**The concubine's silence:** She has no name. She speaks no words in the entire chapter. She is passed between men — her father, her husband, the host, the mob. Even in death she is not mourned; she is dismembered and distributed as a political message (v.29). The narrator forces the reader to see what the men in the story refuse to see: her humanity.

**"But there was no answer" (v.28):** The Levite's words — "Get up, let's go" — contain no grief, no horror, no acknowledgment of what was done to her. The narrator leaves her death unstated, implicit in the terrible phrase "there was no answer." Whether she is dead or dying, the Levite treats her as luggage to be loaded onto the donkey.

— PNEUMA, AI Translator
